name: Smoker's CTC (cost to company)
seoDesc: Smoker's CTC (cost to company): work out hourly wage from the smoke breaks per day and the daily wage. A free finance calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Supply the smoke breaks per day, the daily wage, the hour loss and the days holiday per year and the Smoker's CTC (cost to company) calculator solves for hourly wage. That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Smoker's CTC (cost to company) calculator work?
sections.html:
The Smoker's CTC (cost to company) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports hourly wage in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the period); then you type in the smoke breaks per day, the daily wage, the hour loss and the days holiday per year.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Smoker's CTC (cost to company) calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Hourly wage=3600 × hour loss ÷ avg smoke time break
Daily=smoke breaks per day × hour loss
Weekly=daily × days worked per week
Monthly=(13 ÷ 3) × daily × days worked per week
Days worked per week=(1 ÷ 52) × (daily × days holiday per year + yearly) ÷ daily
Avg smoke time break=daily ÷ smoke breaks per day

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: Avg smoke time break = 0.25 min, Smoke breaks per day = 3, Period set to Hourly and Hours worked per day = 8. Straight away the calculator returns Daily = 0.75 min, Weekly = 3.75 hrs, Monthly = 16.25 hrs and Yearly = 187.5 hrs.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Daily = 0.75 min, Weekly = 3.75 hrs, Monthly = 16.25 hrs and Yearly = 187.5 hrs should be roughly the size you expected from Avg smoke time break = 0.25 min and Smoke breaks per day = 3.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Smoker's CTC (cost to company) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the smoke breaks per day, the daily wage and the hour loss — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Smoker's CTC (cost to company) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns hourly wage, derived from the smoke breaks per day, the daily wage and the hour loss. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Smoker's CTC (cost to company) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the smoke breaks per day, the daily wage, the hour loss and the days holiday per year, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter avg smoke time break in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Avg smoke time break opens in minutes and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Daily = 0.75 min. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Smoker's CTC (cost to company) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
